title: Mamata Rallies INDIA Bloc for Unity as TMC Split Deepens Ahead of Monsoon Session
excerpt: Despite losing 20 MPs to a rebel faction and three Rajya Sabha members to the BJP, Mamata Banerjee is pushing opposition parties to close ranks against the ruling alliance as Parliament's monsoon session begins.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Twenty TMC MPs merged with NCPI, supporting the BJP-led NDA.
  • Opposition staged a walkout at an all-party meeting over rebel faction recognition.
  • Mamata Banerjee led a meeting of 23 opposition parties to strategize against the government.

Article summary
  • Twenty TMC MPs merged with the Nationalist Citizens Party of India (NCPI) and extended support to the BJP-led NDA, while three former Rajya Sabha MPs formally joined the BJP and are contesting the July 24 bypolls.
  • Opposition parties staged a symbolic walkout from the July 19 all-party meeting to protest the government's invitation to the rebel NCPI faction before Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla has recognised its status.
  • Mamata Banerjee attended the INDIA bloc's "Janbandhan" meeting alongside 23 opposition parties, which announced bi-monthly coordination meetings and plans to challenge the government on NEET paper leaks and the Ayodhya temple fund controversy.

As India's monsoon session of Parliament opened on July 20, the political landscape in West Bengal and at the national opposition level is being reshaped by the most consequential split in the Trinamool Congress since its founding in 1998.

Mamata Banerjee, the party's founder-chairperson and former Chief Minister of West Bengal, is waging a two-front battle: holding her fractured party together while rallying the broader INDIA opposition alliance against the BJP-led government. It is a balancing act that carries implications for Indian democratic politics well beyond Kolkata.

A Party Torn Apart After Bengal's Election Shock

The TMC's crushing defeat in the 2026 West Bengal Assembly elections — which brought the BJP to power in the state for the first time under Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari — exposed fault lines that had been building for years. Banerjee herself lost her Bhabanipur constituency to Adhikari, her former protégé turned political rival.

https://x.com/PTI_News/status/2079496144145780979

The fallout was swift. Within weeks, the party split into two factions: one led by Mamata and her nephew Abhishek Banerjee, and another by rebel MLAs Ritabrata Banerjee and Sandipan Saha. The rebel camp secured the support of 60 MLAs, enough to install Ritabrata as Leader of Opposition in the West Bengal Assembly, according to Wikipedia's account of the crisis.

The rupture spread to Parliament. Twenty TMC Lok Sabha MPs, led by veteran parliamentarian Kakoli Ghosh Dastidar, broke away and announced a merger with the Tripura-based Nationalist Citizens Party of India (NCPI). The rebel group has extended formal support to the BJP-led National Democratic Alliance.

"It makes no difference. Elected representatives derive their mandate from Mamata Banerjee and the people. Those leaving could be motivated by fear or greed."

— Dola Sen, TMC MP

Separately, three former TMC Rajya Sabha MPs — Sukhendu Sekhar Roy, Sushmita Dev, and Prakash Chik Baraik — resigned from both the party and their parliamentary seats, then formally joined the BJP. The party immediately fielded all three as candidates for the July 24 Rajya Sabha bypolls, according to The Indian Eye.

Opposition Unites — at Least on Paper

Even as her own party haemorrhages, Banerjee has doubled down on opposition unity at the national level. She attended the INDIA bloc's "Janbandhan" meeting at Delhi's Constitution Club alongside representatives of 23 opposition parties. The gathering agreed on five key decisions, including bi-monthly coordination meetings and a letter to the Chief Justice of India on what the bloc calls "vote loot," according to Republic TV's coverage. The alliance also demanded the resignation of Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan over the NEET-UG paper leak scandal.

The show of unity faced visible cracks. The DMK, the Congress's key ally in Tamil Nadu, boycotted the meeting amid a deepening rift with the national party. The Aam Aadmi Party also stayed away. BJP leaders were quick to dismiss the gathering, with Sambit Patra calling it a "paper alliance" that had already dissolved.

Walkout Sets Combative Tone for Parliament

The opposition's combative posture was on full display at the customary all-party meeting on July 19, just a day before the monsoon session began. Multiple opposition parties walked out to protest the government's decision to invite representatives of the rebel NCPI faction, arguing that the group's recognition was still pending before Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla.

"The entire opposition is united, no matter how much the government tries to engineer defections or create divisions."

— Dharmendra Yadav, Samajwadi Party MP

Congress MP Jairam Ramesh described the NCPI as a "parking place" for 20 rebel TMC MPs and said even the DMK and AAP, which had skipped the Janbandhan meeting, joined the walkout, according to The Business Standard. CPI(M) leader John Brittas said the "sanctity of the all-party meeting has been sullied."

The monsoon session, running from July 20 to August 13, is expected to see the opposition aggressively raise the Ayodhya temple funds controversy, the NEET paper leak case, and questions about what they describe as government-engineered defections.

What It Means for the Indian Diaspora

For the Indian diaspora, the TMC split and opposition realignment carry political and cultural significance — West Bengal has one of the largest overseas communities, and the state's politics under Mamata Banerjee have long shaped conversations in NRI networks about governance, identity, and democratic accountability in India.

What Comes Next

The immediate test is the July 24 Rajya Sabha bypolls, where the three former TMC leaders now running on BJP tickets will gauge voter sentiment. The larger question is whether the INDIA bloc can sustain its unity through a contentious monsoon session and beyond, or whether the centrifugal forces pulling at its seams — from TMC defections to DMK boycotts — prove too strong for even Mamata Banerjee's considerable political will to overcome.
